interviewQuestions.question: How would you extend this design to a multi-seller marketplace with split shipments?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start from what changes structurally: a single customer order can now span multiple sellers, and each seller only fulfills their own items. So I'd add a `sellerId` onto each `OrderItem` at checkout time (itself part of the snapshot, since a seller's item catalog is theirs), and introduce a `Shipment` per seller rather than per order — the existing shipment-as-a-separate-entity design from the base case study already supports multiple shipments against one order, so this is really the same mechanism used more heavily.

Payment gets more interesting: I'd still capture one payment from the customer for the whole order total, then split settlement to each seller afterward based on their items' snapshotted prices minus platform fees — that split-payout logic is a separate concern from the cart/order model itself.

I'd flag returns as the trickiest part: a return now has to route back to the specific seller who fulfilled that item, not the platform as a whole.

**Testing:** whether you can extend an existing model by adding fields and reusing entities, rather than redesigning the order/shipment relationship from scratch.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Multi-seller marketplace orders

interviewQuestions.question: Why must an order's line items be immutable snapshots instead of live references to the product catalog?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd anchor the answer in what an order actually represents: a legal and financial record of what was charged at a specific point in time, not a live view of the catalog. If `OrderItem` just referenced `Product` and read its current price, a price change or rename next month would silently rewrite what every past order appears to show — which breaks receipts, breaks returns/refund math, and in most places isn't even compliant for a completed sale.

I'd give the concrete failure case: a customer paid $40 for a shirt, the price rises to $45 next week, and their order history now shows $45 — a support nightmare and a real accounting discrepancy since $40 is what was actually charged and reconciled against payment.

The fix is copying every fact the order needs — name, price, chosen options — onto the `OrderItem` at checkout, so the order is self-contained and correct forever regardless of what happens to the catalog afterward.

**Testing:** whether you recognize when a record needs to freeze a point-in-time fact instead of defaulting to a live foreign-key reference.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why snapshot instead of reference
